title: The inner critic and its policeman
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Which voice speaks most in your head: critic, praiser or ideal self?

Jose said that from early on our parents develop a little voice: good boy, good girl, bad boy, bad girl. It becomes our inner critic. He described three parts: the ideal self image, the inner praiser and the inner critic, and said that a famous psychologist called this the superego. That naming is Jose's and needs a person to check it.
A student said: probably all problems stem from that.
Jose said that if you go down the critical path, I am not good enough, I should have made more money, you can pummel yourself. A student said: you have no defense, because it is your own voice.
Jose suggested picturing a policeman that says: stop beating yourself up, stop second-guessing yourself. Then the positive voice says: engage, enjoy what you love, and go in the right direction.

Jose said that the inner critic can show a distorted slice of reality, a survival pattern. We may then ask somebody else, whose view is also distorted, and decide from insecurity and not from resourcefulness.
What would your policeman say to your critic?
Education, not advice. If this is heavy for you, a trained person can help.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write what your inner critic says most.
Write what your inner praiser would say.
Write what your ideal self would do.
Write the sentence your policeman says to stop the critic.
Write who you could ask who is not distorted.

check.q: What did Jose say becomes the inner critic?
What did a student say about defending against the critic?
choices: You have no defense, it is your own voice

recap: Hear the three voices. Interrupt the critic. Choose from resourcefulness.
